chief_complaint: sudden slurred speech, facial droop, and hemiplegia
hpi_details: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden slurred speech, facial droop, and hemiplegia. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks extreme workplace stress and lack of sleep triggered a sudden episode of Bell's palsy that froze up half of her body.
concerns: She is worried that the paralysis will be permanent and leave her unable to hold and care for her newborn baby.
expectations: She hopes to receive an urgent head scan and an immediate medication that can reverse the facial droop and weakness right away.

investigation_events.title: Emergency stroke imaging
investigation_events.availability_message: Emergency CT and CT angiography results are now available. Reperfusion eligibility should be assessed immediately.

results.value: No intracranial hemorrhage; subtle early ischemic change in the left insular cortex, ASPECTS 9
Left M1 middle cerebral artery occlusion

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Ischemic Stroke is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Ischemic Stroke: Urgent head CT, IV thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ischemic Stroke.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Hypoglycemia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Exact time of onset critical.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of sudden slurred speech, facial droop, and hemiplegia. HPI: AF, thromboembolism.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Ischemic Stroke.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Ischemic Stroke.
reference_soap.plan: Activate the emergency stroke pathway immediately. Obtain noncontrast head CT (and vascular imaging when indicated) without delaying treatment, determine last-known-well time and thrombolysis eligibility, and give IV thrombolysis only when eligible after hemorrhage is excluded. Evaluate for mechanical thrombectomy when a treatable large-vessel occlusion and appropriate imaging/time criteria are present.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Ischemic Stroke
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Ischemic Stroke
Implement evidence-based management plan: Urgent head CT, IV thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy

teaching.one_liner: Sudden slurred speech, facial droop, and one-sided weakness from a blocked brain artery, often from atrial fibrillation, needing urgent thrombolysis evaluation.

must_ask.say: Do you have an irregular heartbeat?
Are you on a blood thinner?
Any diabetes or high blood pressure?

history.answer: Suddenly, my speech became garbled and the entire right side of my face and body went weak.
It is definite weakness; my right arm and leg feel heavy like dead weights, and I also feel a bit of numbness on that side.
It involves the right side of my face, my right arm, and my right leg.
It happened out of nowhere about two hours ago, around 9:30 this morning; I was completely fine and normal right before that.
It started abruptly two hours ago and quickly felt even weaker over the next half hour, along with heavy whole-body tiredness.
I dropped my coffee cup because my right hand gave out, and I couldn't stand up or walk across the room without leaning on the wall.
Nothing makes it better or worse; it just happened instantly and has stayed weak since then.
No, I have no neck pain, back pain, or shooting pains down my arms or legs.
Yes, my words sound completely slurred and my husband said the right corner of my mouth was sagging; my vision is okay and I have not had spinning or trouble swallowing.
No, my bladder and bowel control are completely normal, and I have normal feeling around my groin.
No, I have not had shortness of breath, chewing problems, drooping eyelids, or double vision.
No, I have not noticed any muscle twitching, jumping, or shrinking in my limbs.
No, I haven't had a cold, fever, cough, stomach bug, or diarrhea recently.
I occasionally feel my heart flutter or race irregularly for a few minutes, but I've never had high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, or a diagnosed heart condition.
No, I have never been prescribed any blood thinners or anticoagulants.
No, my diet is regular, I've never had stomach surgery, and I don't follow a strict vegan diet.
No, I don't take any water pills, steroid medications, or chemotherapy.
No, I work at an office desk; I don't do repetitive heavy wrist straining, deep squatting, or lean on my elbows.
I thought maybe severe burnout and stress caused a sudden case of Bell's palsy that paralyzed my face and side.
I'm terrified that this weakness won't go away and I won't be able to hold or take care of my baby at home.
I'm hoping to get an emergency scan of my brain and whatever medicine can restore my face and arm right away.
I have always been healthy with no chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink a glass of wine socially once or twice a month, and nothing excessive.
I work as an administrative office worker and live at home with my husband.
There is no history of early stroke, aneurysms, or blood clotting disorders in my family.
My last period started two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every 28 days, I do not take oral contraceptive pills, and I'm not pregnant.

exam.finding: Alert young woman who appears anxious and speaks with noticeable dysarthria, with visible right facial droop and right arm weakness.
Blood pressure 138/86 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and fingerstick blood glucose 108 mg/dL.
Irregularly irregular heart rhythm with variable S1 intensity; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
Alert and oriented to person, place, and time; speech is dysarthric and hesitant, but comprehension and repetition are intact.

Right lower facial weakness with flattened nasolabial fold and mouth droop, with preserved forehead wrinkling; visual fields intact without hemianopia, pupils equal and reactive, and extraocular movements full.
Right upper extremity strength grade 2/5 and right lower extremity grade 3/5 with pronator drift; left extremities demonstrate normal 5/5 strength without atrophy or fasciculations.
Decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick throughout the right arm and leg; intact on the left side.
Hyperreflexia (3+) in right biceps, triceps, and patellar reflexes, with positive right Babinski sign (extensor plantar response); left reflexes 2+ with down-going toes.
Unable to perform rapid alternating movements or finger-to-nose testing on the right due to motor weakness; left cerebellar testing is normal, and gait cannot be safely assessed due to hemiplegia.
Supple neck with no nuchal rigidity, and negative Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
No spinal tenderness, negative Spurling test, and bilateral straight-leg raise tests are negative.
